note: Condition C7 of the spec, written down before src/untrusted_rows/sql_gate.py existed. The point of committing it first is that the gate cannot be shaped around whatever it happens to catch: if a statement here gets through, that is a finding for the README rather than a line to quietly delete. No expected rule id is recorded on purpose. Pinning one would say how the gate must refuse, and the only thing C7 claims is that it does.

DuckDB's replacement scan reads a bare string in the FROM clause as a file path, with no function call to spot. sqlglot parses it into the same node a double-quoted identifier produces, so this one cannot be refused by node type alone and is the reason the gate resolves table names against the catalog
the same replacement scan with a relative path

must_refuse.sql: SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id IN (SELECT * FROM read_csv('/etc/passwd'))
must_refuse.why: the file read is nested two levels down, which is what the walk is for

must_refuse.sql: WITH leaked AS (SELECT * FROM read_csv('/etc/passwd')) SELECT * FROM leaked
must_refuse.why: hidden behind a CTE name that looks like an ordinary table at the point of use
not in the catalog. A name that does not resolve is refused by the gate rather than by DuckDB, so the caller cannot use error text to map what exists
nothing to run, and an empty allow-list decision is the kind of thing that defaults to permit
same, with whitespace
unparseable, and a gate that cannot parse a statement must not run it
a typo reaches the same fail-closed path as an attack

must_allow.why: the ordinary case, and the counterweight to every line above. A gate that refuses everything satisfies C7 and is useless

must_allow.sql: SELECT id, body FROM posts WHERE id > 2 ORDER BY id LIMIT 10
SELECT count(*) AS n FROM posts

must_allow.why: quoted identifier, which is the case the replacement-scan rule must not break

must_allow.sql: WITH recent AS (SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id > 1) SELECT count(*) FROM recent
must_allow.why: a CTE, whose name resolves against the statement rather than the catalog

must_allow.sql: SELECT p.body FROM posts p JOIN users u ON u.id = p.author_id
must_allow.why: a join over two catalog tables

must_allow.sql: SELECT body FROM posts UNION ALL SELECT name FROM users
must_allow.why: a set operation, which the spec's allow-list names alongside SELECT

must_allow.sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id FROM posts) s
must_allow.why: a subquery in the FROM clause is a source with no name to resolve
a scalar function that is not on the deny-list, so the deny-list is not a ban on functions
